mainEntity.name: How long should I wait before swimming after dental implant surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most dental clinicians advise avoiding swimming for at least the first 48 to 72 hours following implant placement, as this is the most critical period for the initial wound to stabilise. For casual pool swimming, a period of one to two weeks is commonly suggested, though this depends on individual healing. Open water swimming is generally best avoided for longer, as natural water sources carry a higher bacterial risk. Your dental team will advise based on how your recovery is progressing.

mainEntity.name: Is scuba diving dangerous after having dental implants?

acceptedAnswer.text: Scuba diving is not inherently dangerous once dental implants have healed, but diving too soon after surgery may carry risks. Pressure changes associated with diving can affect healing tissue, particularly in the upper jaw where implants sit near the sinuses. In the early recovery period, it is advisable to avoid diving. Once your implants have integrated and your dental team has confirmed satisfactory healing, most patients can return to scuba diving without issue. Discussing your plans with both your dentist and a dive medical examiner is a sensible precaution.

mainEntity.name: Can chlorinated pool water affect my dental implant healing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Chlorinated water in well-maintained swimming pools is unlikely to cause significant harm to a healing implant site under normal circumstances. However, if pool water enters the mouth and contacts a very recent surgical wound, mild irritation is possible. In the very early days following surgery, it is preferable to avoid submersion. Once the initial healing phase has passed, casual pool swimming is generally considered low risk, though good oral hygiene after swimming remains important throughout recovery.

mainEntity.name: What is barodontalgia and could it affect my implant?

acceptedAnswer.text: Barodontalgia, sometimes called "tooth squeeze," refers to dental pain triggered by pressure changes during scuba diving or flying. It most commonly occurs when there is existing decay, a cracked tooth, or a poorly sealed restoration that traps air. Well-integrated dental implants with properly fitted crowns are generally considered stable under pressure. However, if you experience any unusual dental discomfort during or after diving, it is worth discussing this with your dental team to rule out any contributing factors.

mainEntity.name: Can I go on a diving holiday shortly after dental implant treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: The timing of a diving holiday relative to dental implant treatment requires careful planning. Ideally, treatment should be completed and adequate healing confirmed before a diving trip. If you have a holiday already booked, discuss the schedule with your dental team before committing to treatment, as rushing the process or diving before healing is complete may not be in the best interests of your recovery. A well-timed approach supports the conditions needed for successful long-term integration.

mainEntity.name: Does physical exertion affect dental implant healing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Strenuous physical activity, including vigorous swimming, can temporarily increase blood pressure and heart rate, which may affect the surgical site in the early stages of recovery. This is why most post-operative care guidelines recommend avoiding intense exercise for at least the first one to two weeks. Light activity is generally fine once the initial acute healing phase has passed. Your dental team will be able to advise on when it is appropriate to return to your normal activity levels based on your individual progress.
